lead: A CUDA program has two parts: host code that runs on the CPU and kernels that run on the GPU. A kernel is a function launched over a grid of blocks, and each block holds a fixed number of threads. Every thread computes its own global index from built-in variables, then works on one array element. This structure lets one launch cover thousands of independent data items. It is used in image filters, matrix multiplication, neural-network training and any loop whose iterations do not depend on each other.
prereq: You need: the GPU execution model from Chapter 3.3.

blocks.text: A CUDA source file mixes two kinds of code. Host code runs on the CPU. Device code runs on the GPU. A function marked __global__ is a kernel: the host launches it, and many GPU threads run the same body. A function marked __device__ is called only from GPU code. A function marked __host__ is ordinary CPU code, which is the default. Kernels must return void.

The launch syntax is kernel<<>>(arguments). The first slot gives grid dimensions, the second gives block dimensions. For a 1D launch of 2 blocks with 4 threads each, write add<<<2, 4>>>(dA, dB, dC). The host first allocates device arrays and copies input data. Then it launches the kernel. Then it copies the result back. The memory copies are covered in Chapter 3.6.

nvcc, the NVIDIA CUDA compiler, compiles the file. It splits host code for the CPU compiler and device code for the GPU. A typical command is nvcc add.cu -o add. The host code cannot read a device pointer directly; device memory is a separate address space. The pointer arguments passed to a kernel must point to device memory. The kernel itself does not allocate global arrays; the host does that before launch.

CUDA gives each thread four built-in variables. gridDim.x is the number of blocks in the grid along x. blockDim.x is the number of threads in one block along x. blockIdx.x is the block number, from 0 to gridDim.x − 1. threadIdx.x is the thread number inside its block, from 0 to blockDim.x − 1. The fields .x, .y and .z allow 1D, 2D or 3D layouts.

blocks.where: i is the global array index; blockIdx.x is the block number; blockDim.x is the number of threads per block; threadIdx.x is the thread number inside its block.

blocks.text: With blockDim.x = 4, block 0 gives i = 0,1,2,3 and block 1 gives i = 4,5,6,7. Every thread gets a different i, so threads do not collide. For 2D data such as an image of width W, use column = blockIdx.x × blockDim.x + threadIdx.x and row = blockIdx.y × blockDim.y + threadIdx.y. The flat index is i = row × W + column. This row-major order matches a C array stored row by row. A launch of dim3 grid(2,3) and dim3 block(16,16) therefore has 2 × 3 = 6 blocks and 16 × 16 = 256 threads per block.

sections.h3: Bounds checks and two common patterns

blocks.text: A launch often rounds the block count up. If N = 10 and blockDim.x = 4, you need ceil(10/4) = 3 blocks, which gives 12 threads. Threads with i = 10 and i = 11 have no array element. Guard every access with if (i < N) { ... }. Without this check, the extra threads read or write past the array. The write may corrupt another variable, or the read may return garbage.

The map pattern gives each thread one output element: C[i] = A[i] + B[i]. The kernel body is short, and the grid supplies all parallelism. A grid-stride loop handles arrays larger than one launch: for (int i = blockIdx.x*blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; i < N; i += blockDim.x*gridDim.x) { ... }. Each thread processes several elements with the same index formula.

The reduce pattern combines many values into one. A simple version has each thread load one element, then threads in a block combine partial results. The final result may need one more pass over per-block partials. Shared memory makes the in-block part faster; that memory space is described in Chapter 3.5. Bounds checks remain necessary in both patterns whenever N is not an exact multiple of the block size.

figure.caption: Each column is one thread of the 2 × 4 launch, and it adds one pair of elements. The marked column is thread 1 of block 1: i = 1 × 4 + 1 = 5, so it writes C[5] = 13 + 3 = 16.

examples.question: The arrays A = [2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19] and B = [1,1,2,2,3,3,4,4] have N = 8 elements. A kernel is launched with gridDim.x = 2 and blockDim.x = 4. Using the 1D global index, compute every C[i] = A[i] + B[i]. Show the index for each thread.
steps: Global index for block b and thread t is i = b × 4 + t.
Every i from 0 to 7 is used exactly once, so the full result is C = [3,4,7,9,14,16,21,23].

traps: Launching ceil(N/blockDim.x) blocks but testing i <= N instead of i < N, so one thread writes past the array.
Swapping gridDim and blockDim when computing i; the global index becomes wrong for almost every thread, including nonzero threadIdx values in block 0.
Forgetting that a __global__ kernel must return void; writing int kernel(...) fails at compile time.
Passing a host array pointer directly to a kernel; the device cannot read host memory through that pointer.
In 2D, using i = row + col instead of row*width + col; rows overlap and results are wrong.

quiz.q: What is the difference between __host__ and __device__ functions?
quiz.a: __host__ code runs on the CPU. __device__ code runs on the GPU and is called from GPU code.

quiz.q: Which built-in variable gives the number of threads in one block along x?
Why does the 1D global index multiply blockIdx.x by blockDim.x?
quiz.a: Blocks own consecutive groups of blockDim.x indices, so block b starts at b*blockDim.x; adding threadIdx.x gives the position inside that group.

quiz.q: A launch has gridDim.x = 3 and blockDim.x = 5. Find i for blockIdx.x = 2 and threadIdx.x = 4. For N = 14, is this i valid?
quiz.a: i = 2*5 + 4 = 14. It is valid only if i < 14, so for N = 14 it is invalid.

quiz.q: N = 10 and blockDim.x = 4. How many blocks are launched with ceil(N/blockDim.x)? Which thread indices are invalid?
quiz.a: ceil(10/4) = 3 blocks, giving 12 threads. The invalid indices are i = 10 and i = 11, so the kernel needs the guard i < 10.

quiz.q: For N = 8, compare the launches <<<1,8>>> and <<<8,1>>>. Do they produce the same global indices? Why might performance differ?
quiz.a: Both give i = 0 to 7. <<<1,8>>> has one block of 8 threads, so only one block is available to occupy an SM. <<<8,1>>> has eight blocks of one thread, which wastes warp lanes and adds block scheduling. Neither uses full warps well, but block size and block count change occupancy.

quiz.q: A kernel writes C[i] without if (i < N). N = 1000, blockDim.x = 256 and gridDim.x = 4. How many threads launch and which writes are out of bounds?
quiz.a: 4*256 = 1024 threads launch. The writes for i = 1000 to 1023 are out of bounds, so 1023 − 1000 + 1 = 24 writes go past C.

beyond: Not for the exam. CUDA's grid, block and thread vocabulary reappears in HIP, SYCL, OpenCL and GPU libraries, so the index formula transfers almost unchanged. Production kernels add grid-stride loops, occupancy tuning and cooperative groups for block-wide synchronization. Newer curricula also show Triton and CUDA C++ templates that generate launch configurations. Search next for CUDA occupancy, grid-stride loop and cooperative groups.
